blocks.text: The letter commends Gaius because travelers have testified that he lives faithfully in the truth. His practical care for fellow believers, including people previously unknown to him, is treated as part of that faithfulness. The elder asks him to help such travelers continue their journey and says that welcoming them makes others fellow-workers for the truth.

The travelers are described as going out “for the Name,” an expression the letter itself does not further explain, and as accepting nothing from the Gentiles or nations. The elder therefore presents support for them as a responsibility of those within the believing community. Their report of Gaius’s love before the church gives concrete content to the earlier praise of his walk in truth.

The conflict with Diotrephes is specific: the elder says that Diotrephes refuses to receive the elder’s representatives, speaks maliciously against them, prevents others from receiving the fellow believers, and puts supporters out of the church. The instruction to imitate good rather than evil follows this account. By contrast, Demetrius is introduced with testimony from everyone, from “the truth itself,” and from the elder and his associates.

The sender calls himself simply “the elder,” addressing Gaius as beloved. Though he has more to say, he prefers not to use ink and pen; he expects to see Gaius soon and speak face to face. The closing exchange of peace and named greetings keeps the letter’s concerns within a network of personal relationships.

3 John belongs alongside writings that share concentrated vocabulary, formulas, and concerns with 1 John, 2 John, and the Fourth Gospel. That relationship may help explain why this brief personal letter uses familiar themes such as truth, love, testimony, and walking faithfully.
